note: Read from tree-sitter-haskell's scanner.c (3471 lines, the largest of the
eight) and from the Haskell 2010 Report §10.3. This book claims none of the
layout: `writ` already executes the `_cmd_*` orders and answers the `_cond_*`
layout questions against the same stack, under the unanimity warrant its own
header sets out, and it does that correctly. What `writ` cannot reach is the
OTHER family of blind externals here - the twenty-odd `_cond_*` terminals that
are zero-width conditions on the BYTES around a symbolic operator - because a
`Provision` is a pattern and these are questions about a maximal operator run,
the whitespace in front of it, and which of several conditions the parse would
take.
The dot family is where that costs the most, and `inquest.zig`'s own header
names the exhibit: state 7 of `module Text.Pandoc.Shared` admits
`_cond_qual_dot` and `_cond_tight_dot` by shift, and with neither answerable
every qualified name in a Haskell file walls at its first `.`. On the pandoc
corpus that is the whole import section, which is why the `where` further down
the file came back as `variable`: not a phantom, not layout, just a parse that
had already fallen into a forest by line three.
Every rule here is zero width. The grammar spells each condition as
`SEQ(_cond_X, ".")` - the scanner says which reading of the dot this is and
the ordinary lexer still eats the byte - so the answer's whole content is its
name, and `emit … 0` is the literal reading of the C's `mark_end` before the
operator.
Deliberately not here: `_varsym` / `_consym` and the section family
(`_cond_left_section_op`, `_cond_no_section_op`, `_cond_qualified_op`,
`_cond_minus`, `_cond_infix`, `_cond_data_infix`, `_cond_context`,
`_cond_assoc_tyinst`). Those are not zero width and their guards run a second
lookahead past the operator (`left_section_op` looks for the `)` that makes
`(1 - 2 +)` a section), which the algebra can state but which needs its own
reading to state correctly.
Also not here, and this one is a boundary rather than a deferral: the `where`
that came back as `variable` is not a scanner question at all. It is the
Report's `parse-error(t)`, and it needed the layout STACK - which `writ` owns,
not this book's `frames` organ. `writ` grew the arm (`outside.tailed`), derived
from the grammar's own literal terminals rather than from a keyword list, and
it took haskell from 137 misread bytes to 11. `WHERE` appears exactly once in
scanner.c outside its enum, as `valid(env, WHERE)` in `end_layout_where`, and
that single line is the whole rule: a keyword the parse refuses ends the block.
The five `_phantom_*` stay declined for the reason `writ`'s header gives.

rules.name: dotdot
rules.note: scanner.c:2761-2763. `lex_symop` calls the run `LDotDot` when it is exactly two characters and both are dots, so the negative lookahead is what makes the run maximal - `...` is `LDotSymop` and belongs to the qualified rule below. DOTDOT is tried before the tight reading and does not care whether whitespace preceded it, which is the one member of this family that does not.

rules.name: tight_dot
rules.note: scanner.c:2764-2765, the `!whitespace` half. `A.b` is a qualified name or a field selector; the lookbehind IS the C's `whitespace` flag, which is set by the prologue that skipped the blanks before this run. A lookbehind rather than a fact because the fact is about the byte before the offset and nothing on `Facts` says that.

rules.name: prefix_dot
rules.note: scanner.c:2764-2765, the `whitespace` half. ` .field` with a space in front is the record dot selector, which is a prefix operator rather than a qualification.

rules.name: prefix_dot_open
rules.note: scanner.c:2769-2770 with `opening_token` at 2040. `LDotOpen` is a lone dot in front of something a term can start with; `is_id_char` is already the rule above, so what is left is `(`, `[`, `"` and a `{` that does not open a comment. Without whitespace the C falls through to VARSYM, which this book does not claim - so the tight half is silence rather than a wrong answer.

rules.name: qual_dot
rules.note: scanner.c:2763, 2766, 2768 - all three arms end in `tight_op(env, whitespace, QUAL_DOT)`, so one rule states the union: a dot with no whitespace in front of it whose run is not a lone dot and which is not standing before a bracket. `A.B.c`, `A.B.C` and `A.B.+` are all this, which is why the qualified reading has to admit a symop after the dot where the tight reading admits only an identifier. Ordered behind the three above because the C tries each of them first and only falls through to here.

rules.name: left_section_operator
rules.note: scanner.c:2222-2230, reached through `finish_symop` at 2251-2259. `(1 - 2 +)` cannot be decided on one lookahead token: the parser must know whether to reduce `1 - 2` as a section's operand or shift another infix. So the scanner looks PAST the operator run for the `)` and says which. `char_at(env, start, ')')` indexes the lookahead buffer from the token start, not from where `skip_whitespace` left the position, so the paren has to stand immediately after the run - which is why the operator class excluding `)` already makes the run maximal here.

rules.name: no_section_operator
rules.note: scanner.c:2227. The auxiliary the comment at 2217 explains: this arm has already advanced over the whitespace behind the operator, so a following step would either swallow that whitespace into its extent or answer zero-width. Emitting NO_SECTION_OP instead retires LEFT_SECTION_OP for the next ask and leaves every other infix operator valid, so the run comes back as a varsym on the re-ask. Ordered behind the section rule because the C tests the paren first and only then the gap.

rules.name: consym
rules.note: scanner.c:2780. `LSymop` whose first byte is `:` is a constructor operator, and the extent is the whole maximal run because `symop_lookahead` consumed it before `MARK`. This is the rule the board was waiting on: `first:splitBy isSep rest` walled at its `:` on line 131 of the pandoc fixture, and a file that cannot lex cons cannot build a list anywhere.

rules.name: varsym
rules.note: scanner.c:2781. Everything else `lex_symop` calls `LSymop`, which is the DEFAULT arm of a classifier with eleven special cases - so the guard is `no_probe sym_routed`, stating those eleven once rather than restating the default. Five of them are conditional on the byte AFTER the operator, not on the operator: `lex_prefix` returns its special reading only when an `opening_token` follows and otherwise falls back to `LSymop`, and `lex_splice` the same for a varid or `(`. So `f $ x` and `a ! b` are varsyms while `$x` is a splice and `f !x` is a bang, and a book that routed the byte unconditionally lost the most common operator in Haskell. `f . g` reaches here too: a lone dot with neither an identifier nor an opening token behind it is composition, and the dot rules above already claim the two readings that are qualification.
